quote: Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.
source: Herman Melville, Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, chapter 1, Loomings, the opening paragraph (Ishmael) (Harper and Brothers, 1851)
speaker: Ishmael
note: Corrected: the proposal cut the sentence with an ellipsis and raised a lowercase whenever to a capital. The whole sentence is given as the 1851 text prints it, so nothing between the November mood and the remedy of the sea is hidden.

evidence.where: Project Gutenberg text of Moby-Dick (ebook 2701), fetched and read this run, chapter 1, Loomings, the first paragraph read in full; the same sentence was verified against the same text in month 7 (07-cfl-05)
evidence.edition: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, Harper and Brothers, New York, 1851, in the standard text carried by Project Gutenberg
evidence.locator: chapter 1, Loomings, first paragraph, the sentence beginning Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth

reason: The words are real, but the elided version was rejected in month 7 because the ellipsis hid about sixty words of the passage's own reason for the mood, and this proposal repeats the same cut with a minted capital. The uncut sentence is honest and on theme for November: coffin warehouses and funerals are mortality, and going to sea is the remedy, told wryly. The editor should weigh two things: it runs to about ninety words, and the next sentence, not quoted, calls the voyage a substitute for pistol and ball. Melville is at zero of three and not banned.
